834.title: Zayd ibn Thabit
834.hook: the young scribe of revelation who learned new scripts, then gathered the Qur'an
834.howItsDone: Muslims remember Zayd ibn Thabit as a scribe of revelation and the one who gathered the Qur'an into sheets under Abu Bakr, from the reports in Sahih al-Bukhari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who asked did He name me, and wept. Your line was: recite to him. Who did you read to, and did they listen? Day eight hundred thirty-four.

A board, and a pot of ink. That is what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, calls for when a new verse comes. Bring Zayd, he says, and tell him to bring the board and the inkwell. A young man from Medina arrives and sits down to write. Halfway through, a blind companion speaks up from the room, and what happens next changes the words on the board while the ink is still wet. Today: the young man holding the pen.
screen: `A BOARD AND A POT OF INK.` → `BRING ZAYD.` → `A BLIND MAN SPEAKS UP.`

segments.voice: Zayd ibn Thabit was one of the Ansar, and he wrote down revelation for the Prophet. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene from the hook. A verse came saying that believers who sit at home are not equal to those who strive in God's way. Zayd wrote it. Then Ibn Umm Maktum, who was blind, spoke: Messenger of God, if I were able, I would go out too. And before the writing was finished, a few more words came down: except those who have a disability. Zayd added them. The pen was there when the text was still arriving. A second report, which Bukhari mentions, tells that the Prophet asked Zayd to learn the writing of the Jews of Medina, so that he could write the Prophet's letters and read the letters that came back. Zayd learned it. Tradition says he picked it up quickly. So the young scribe became a translator too: a person who learned a new script because his work needed it. Then, years later, comes the task you may remember from Hafsah's day. When Abu Bakr decided to gather the Qur'an into written sheets, he chose Zayd, and Bukhari keeps his reason. You are a wise young man, Abu Bakr told him. We do not suspect you. And you used to write the revelation for the Messenger of God. That one sentence is a whole job description. Young. Sensible. Trusted. And practiced, because he had been at the board with the ink pot all along. Skills learned in small, ordinary moments, one verse at a time, one new alphabet at a time, became the thing the community leaned on.
screen: `THE BOARD AND THE INKWELL.` · `EXCEPT THOSE WHO HAVE A DISABILITY.` · `HE LEARNED A NEW SCRIPT.` · `YOU ARE A WISE YOUNG MAN.` · then, large: `THE YOUNG SCRIBE.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn a new skill. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you've been meaning to learn. A few letters of the Arabic alphabet. A knot. A recipe. A phrase in a neighbor's language. Five chords. Choose one piece of it small enough to start today. Breathe in, and picture yourself as a beginner, slow and clumsy. Breathe out, and let that be fine. If you pray, you can ask that what you learn be useful to someone. The bell holds the time.
Zayd ibn Thabit. The young scribe who wrote down revelation, learned a new script for the Prophet's letters, and was chosen by Abu Bakr to gather the Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: the young scribe. Today, spend ten minutes as a beginner at something new. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

835.title: Mu'adh ibn Jabal
835.hook: sent to Yemen and asked how he would judge: by the book, then the sunnah, then his own reasoning (Abu Dawud)
835.howItsDone: Students of Islamic law learn the hadith of Mu'adh from Sunan Abu Dawud as a picture of how a judge reasons: the Qur'an, then the sunnah, then careful reasoning (ijtihad).

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zayd ibn Thabit, who wrote at the board while the verse was still arriving. Your line was: the young scribe. What did you try as a beginner? Day eight hundred thirty-five.

A man is about to ride south, to Yemen, far from Medina, where he will be the one people bring their quarrels to. There will be no running back to ask. Before he goes, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops him with a question, the kind a teacher asks just before the exam. How will you judge, when a case comes to you? The man's answer is short, and it comes in three steps. Today: Mu'adh ibn Jabal.
screen: `A RIDE SOUTH TO YEMEN.` → `NO RUNNING BACK TO ASK.` → `HOW WILL YOU JUDGE?`

segments.voice: Abu Dawud records the conversation, and it goes in three steps. How will you judge? By the book of God, Mu'adh says. And if you don't find it in the book of God? Then by the sunnah of the Messenger of God. And if you don't find it in the sunnah, or in the book? Then I will use my own reasoning, Mu'adh says, and I will not fall short. And the Prophet, the report says, struck him on the chest and praised God for guiding the messenger of His Messenger to what pleases the Messenger of God. Three steps. The book first. Then the example of the Prophet. And only then, when both are silent on the case in front of you, your own careful thinking, done honestly and with effort. Hadith scholars have discussed the strength of this report's chain, and some accept it while some question it. Its shape is clear, though, and some readers take a habit from it even outside a courtroom: not jumping straight to one's own opinion. First, what has been given. Then, the best example. Then, careful thought. Sahih al-Bukhari adds the advice the Prophet gave Mu'adh and Abu Musa when they set out for Yemen: make things easy, and do not make them hard. Give good news, and do not drive people away. Work together, and do not fall out. A judge with a method, and a gentle way of using it. Book, sunnah, reason.
screen: `FIRST, THE BOOK OF GOD.` · `THEN, THE SUNNAH.` · `THEN, MY OWN REASONING.` · `MAKE THINGS EASY, NOT HARD.` · then, large: `BOOK, SUNNAH, REASON.`

segments.voice: The practice: think before judging. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one judgment you've made recently, or one you're about to make. About a coworker. A family member. A news story. Slow it down into steps. First, what do the facts actually say? Second, what would the wisest person you know do here? Only third, what do you think, now that you've looked? Take a breath for each one. Notice if the judgment softens or sharpens. If you pray, you can ask for fairness in what you decide. The bell holds the time.
Ijtihad, striving, the careful reasoning Mu'adh ibn Jabal said he'd use when the book and the sunnah were both silent, and would not fall short on. Today's word.
Your line: book, sunnah, reason. Today, before you judge one thing, pause and look at what you've been given first. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

836.title: Ibn Abbas
836.hook: the young cousin, prayed for to understand the religion, later the great interpreter (Bukhari)
836.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abdullah ibn Abbas as a companion known for explaining the Qur'an, and retell the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the Prophet prayed for him to be given understanding of the religion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, sent to Yemen with three steps for judging. Your line was: book, sunnah, reason. Did you slow down before one judgment? Day eight hundred thirty-six.

A jug of water has been set out. Nobody asked for it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, comes to wash, finds it waiting, and asks: who put this here? Someone tells him: Abdullah, the son of your uncle Abbas. A boy. He had noticed what would be needed and quietly set it out. And the Prophet, instead of a thank you, says a short prayer for him, one line that the boy will carry for the rest of his life. Today: Ibn Abbas.
screen: `A JUG OF WATER, SET OUT.` → `WHO PUT THIS HERE?` → `A ONE-LINE PRAYER FOR A BOY.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari records the prayer: O God, give him understanding of the religion. In Arabic, the prayer asks that he be given fiqh in the religion, the word later used for the study of Islamic law. In another report in Bukhari, Ibn Abbas says the Prophet held him close and prayed: O God, teach him the book. So the boy was prayed for in both ways: for understanding, and for the Qur'an. Did it show? Bukhari keeps a scene that answers. Years later, Umar, now leading the community, used to bring young Ibn Abbas into his council with the older men who had fought at Badr. Some of them objected. Why does he sit with us, when we have sons his age? So one day Umar asked the whole group about the surah that begins: when the help of God comes, and the victory. Some said it tells us to praise God and seek His forgiveness when victory comes. Others said nothing. Then Umar turned to Ibn Abbas. Is that what you say too? No, he said. It was the sign of the Prophet's own approaching death, given to him by God. When the victory comes, your work is done; praise your Lord and ask forgiveness. Umar answered: I know nothing of it except what you have said. The older men gave the plain meaning, and it was true. The young man saw what the surah was pointing to. Tradition remembers Ibn Abbas as an interpreter of the Qur'an. It started with a jug of water and a one-line prayer. Understanding, prayed for.
screen: `O GOD, GIVE HIM UNDERSTANDING.` · `O GOD, TEACH HIM THE BOOK.` · `UMAR'S QUESTION ABOUT SURAH 110.` · `THE YOUNG MAN UNDERSTOOD.` · then, large: `UNDERSTANDING PRAYED FOR.`

segments.voice: The practice: study one verse's meaning. Settle, and breathe. Take one short verse, maybe the first line of surah one hundred ten, when the help of God comes, and the victory. Say it once, slowly. Then ask Ibn Abbas's kind of question: not only what does it say, but what is it doing? Who is it speaking to? What moment is it for? Sit with that question, without hurrying to an answer. If you pray, you can ask, as the Prophet asked for him, for understanding. The bell holds the time.

Ibn Abbas. Abdullah, son of the Prophet's uncle Abbas, prayed for as a boy to understand the religion and the book, and remembered as an interpreter of the Qur'an. Today's word, and the last of the early believers.

Your line: understanding prayed for. Today, read one verse twice and ask what it is doing, not only what it says. Tomorrow the path turns to the later companions and their stories. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

837.title: Abu Hurayrah
837.hook: named for his little cat, he stayed close and carried the Prophet's words
837.howItsDone: Muslims hear Abu Hurayrah's name at the start of hadith, often followed by 'may God be pleased with him'; some Muslims also take his reports about mercy to animals as a reason to feed and water strays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Abbas, the young cousin the Prophet prayed for. Your line was: understanding prayed for. Which verse did you sit with, and what did it open? Today a new stretch of the road begins: later companions and their stories. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

Father of the little cat. That is what the name means, and he explained it himself. As a boy he looked after his family's flock, and he had a small cat with him. At night he set it in a tree; by day he took it along and played with it. So people started calling him by it. Not by his father's name. By the cat. The report is kept by Tirmidhi. The nickname stuck, and it is the name heard whenever a hadith begins with him. Today: Abu Hurayrah, the companion named for a kitten.
screen: `A BOY, A FLOCK, A SMALL CAT.` → `THEY NAMED HIM FOR THE CAT.` → `ABU HURAYRAH.`

segments.voice: Abu Hurayrah had little to live on, and he made a choice about how to spend his days near the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In Sahih al-Bukhari he answers people who complained that he narrated so much. The emigrants from Mecca, he says, were busy in the markets. The helpers of Medina were busy with their farms and property. He stayed close to the Prophet, content with enough food to keep him going, and so he was there when others were not, and remembered what others missed. In another report he says that once the Prophet told him to spread out his cloak while he spoke, then gather it to his chest, and after that he did not forget. And Bukhari records his own count of himself: none of the companions narrated more than he did, he said, except Abdullah ibn Amr, because Abdullah used to write things down, and he did not. So here is the picture. A man with no trade and no farm, often hungry, who decided that listening was his work. Now put the kitten back in the picture. Among the hadith that reach us through Abu Hurayrah is a story about a man who found a dog panting with thirst, climbed down a well, filled his shoe with water, and gave it a drink. God thanked him, the hadith says, and forgave him. The companions asked whether there is reward even for animals. The answer: in every living creature there is reward. A boy who kept a little cat with him grew into the man who carried that saying.
screen: `LITTLE TO LIVE ON.` · `OTHERS TRADED; HE LISTENED.` · `SPREAD YOUR CLOAK.` · `A DOG, A WELL, A SHOE OF WATER.` · then, large: `FATHER OF THE KITTEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: be kind to a cat. Or a dog, a bird, whatever creature shares your street. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one animal you will pass today. The neighbor's cat on the wall. A bird at the window. Something thirsty on a hot pavement. Breathe in, and see it clearly. Breathe out, and decide one small kindness: fresh water in a bowl, a slower step so you don't startle it, a gentle hand if it wants one. If you pray, you can say bismillah as you set the water down. The bell holds the time.
Abu Hurayrah. A nickname from a little cat, given to a poor companion who stayed close and listened, and through whom the Prophet's sayings still reach us. Today's word.
Your line: father of the kitten. Today, put out water for one creature, or slow down for one, and let a small mercy be part of your name. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

838.title: Anas ibn Malik
838.hook: served the Prophet ten years and never once heard him ask, why did you do that
838.howItsDone: Muslims often cite Anas's report of ten years without a harsh word when teaching about the Prophet's character and about kindness to children, students and anyone who works for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Hurayrah, named for the little cat he carried. Your line was: father of the kitten. Did some creature get water or a gentler step from you? Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

A boy is sent on an errand. He says out loud that he won't go, though inside he means to. He heads out, and on the way through the market he comes upon some children playing, and there he stops. The errand waits. Then a hand takes him gently by the back of the neck. He looks up, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is laughing. Little Anas, he says, did you go where I asked you? And the boy says, yes, I'm going now. That scene is in Sahih Muslim, told by the boy himself. Today: the servant who was never scolded.
screen: `AN ERRAND, AND A GAME.` → `A HAND ON THE NECK.` → `HE WAS LAUGHING.`

segments.voice: Anas ibn Malik came into the Prophet's household as a boy. Bukhari records his mother, Umm Sulaym, saying to the Prophet: Anas is your servant; pray for him. And the Prophet did. So Anas grew up in that house, running errands, watching, listening. Years later he summed up what he had seen in one sentence that both Bukhari and Muslim keep. I served the Prophet for ten years, Anas said, and he never said to me so much as uff. He never said, about something I had done, why did you do that? And never, about something I had left undone, why didn't you do that? Hold that up against an ordinary week. A boy in a busy household, and ten years of jobs. Some were done badly. Some were forgotten. Some, like the errand in the market, were put off while he stopped among children at play. Anas doesn't say he was perfect. He says he was never made to answer for it with a sharp word. And notice the word he picks: uff. Not a lecture. Not a punishment. The smallest sigh of annoyance, the noise people make before they even think. The Qur'an uses that same little word in the surah called the Night Journey, telling believers not to say uff to aging parents. Anas reports that he never heard even that much. Some teachers cite this hadith when they talk about the Prophet's character, and about how to treat anyone who works for you or under you: children, students, staff. Ten years of small failures, met with patience. That is the record a servant kept of his master.
screen: `YOUR SERVANT. PRAY FOR HIM.` · `TEN YEARS IN THE HOUSE.` · `NOT EVEN UFF.` · `NEVER: WHY DID YOU DO THAT?` · then, large: `TEN YEARS, NO SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: The practice: go a day without scolding. Settle, and breathe. Think of the person you are most likely to snap at today. A child, a coworker, someone at the counter, someone at home. See the small thing they might get wrong. The late reply, the dish left out, the job half done. Breathe in, and notice whether an uff starts to rise. Breathe out, and let it go before it reaches your mouth. Choose now what you'll say instead: a question, a joke, or nothing at all. If you pray, you can ask for patience with that one person. The bell holds the time.
Uff, the smallest sigh of annoyance, the word Anas ibn Malik said he never heard in ten years serving the Prophet's house. Today's word.
Your line: ten years, no scolding. Today, when someone gets a small thing wrong, catch the uff before it leaves you, and ask instead of blame. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

839.title: Abdullah ibn Umar
839.hook: followed the Prophet's footsteps so closely he prayed where he had prayed
839.howItsDone: Muslims follow the sunnah, the Prophet's example, in worship and in small daily habits; scholars distinguish acts done as worship from those done by custom, and people differ on how far to follow the second kind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anas ibn Malik, the boy who served in the Prophet's house. Your line was: ten years, no scolding. Did you catch an uff before it got out? Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

On the long road between Medina and Mecca there are spots with nothing special about them. A bend. A tree. A patch of ground by a valley. Travelers pass them without a glance. One traveler kept stopping. Nafi', who learned from him, tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari: Abdullah ibn Umar would halt at certain places along the way and pray there, because he had seen the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, pray in those very places. He simply remembered, and stopped. Today: the son of Umar, walking in someone else's footprints.
screen: `A BEND, A TREE, A VALLEY.` → `HE STOPPED AND PRAYED.` → `BECAUSE THE PROPHET HAD.`

segments.voice: Abdullah was the son of Umar ibn al-Khattab. What his students passed on was how closely he watched, and how closely he copied. Bukhari gives a whole run of reports from Nafi' naming the places on the pilgrimage road where Ibn Umar prayed, each one a spot where the Prophet had prayed before him. Here is another scene, also in Bukhari, that shows what kind of follower he was. As a young man, Abdullah slept in the mosque. He had a dream: two angels took him to the Fire, and he was afraid. He told his sister Hafsah, and she told the Prophet. The Prophet said: what an excellent man Abdullah is, if only he would pray at night. His son Salim adds one line. After that, Abdullah slept only a little of the night. One sentence of praise, with one gentle if only, and it changed the shape of his nights. Later scholars asked what kind of following this was. Some distinguish between what the Prophet did as worship and teaching, and what he did simply as a traveler, such as where he happened to stop. Some readers see Ibn Umar following both kinds, out of love. Either way, the picture stays: a man who wanted his feet to land where the footsteps were.
screen: `THE SON OF UMAR.` · `PLACES ON THE PILGRIM ROAD.` · `IF ONLY HE PRAYED AT NIGHT.` · `WORSHIP, OR JUST WHERE HE STOPPED?` · then, large: `IN HIS FOOTSTEPS.`

segments.voice: The practice: copy one small sunnah, one habit the Prophet is reported to have kept. Settle, and breathe. Choose something small and ordinary. Some Muslims begin with smiling at people they meet, or entering the mosque right foot first, as Ibn Umar himself is reported to have done, or saying bismillah before they eat, or using the right hand to give. You don't have to choose today's most important thing. Choose one you'll actually do. Breathe in, and picture the moment it will happen. Breathe out, and see yourself doing it. If you pray, you can ask to follow well. The bell holds the time.
Abdullah ibn Umar. Son of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who prayed where the Prophet had prayed and, after one if only, rose to pray at night. Today's word.
Your line: in his footsteps. Today, do one small thing the way someone you admire did it, on purpose, and notice how it feels to follow. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

840.title: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf
840.hook: he arrived in Medina with nothing, asked for the market, grew rich, and kept giving
840.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf's reply, 'where is your market?', as a picture of earning with dignity; giving from what one earns, through zakat and voluntary charity, is part of Muslim practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abdullah ibn Umar, who stopped to pray where the Prophet had prayed. Your line was: in his footsteps. Which small sunnah did you copy, and did it stay with you? Day eight hundred forty.

Here is an offer almost too generous to hear. A man has just arrived in Medina from Mecca with nothing. His new brother, a man of the city named Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', says to him: I have more wealth than anyone among the helpers. Take half of it. And I have two wives; see which you like, and I'll divorce her so you can marry. That is in Sahih al-Bukhari. Half of everything, offered to a man who has just arrived. What would anyone say? The newcomer said no. Gently. Today: the man who turned down half a fortune and asked for directions instead.
screen: `A NEWCOMER WITH NOTHING.` → `TAKE HALF OF EVERYTHING.` → `HE SAID NO.`

segments.voice: His name was Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, one of the emigrants. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Medina, he paired emigrants with helpers as brothers, and Abd al-Rahman was paired with Sa'd. Listen to his answer to the offer of half. In Bukhari's report he says: may God bless you in your family and your wealth. Where is your market? And off he went. He traded, the report says, in cheese and butter, and he came back with a profit. Not long after, he turned up with traces of perfume on him, and he told the Prophet he had married. So the first thing to notice is a kind of dignity. He received a huge kindness, blessed the giver, and kept his hands open for work. Then the story goes on. The biographies remember him as becoming very wealthy, and as giving, again and again, in large amounts for the community and its poor. Tradition tells of whole caravans of goods given away; those accounts come from the sira, not from Bukhari, so hold them as stories the tradition tells. And remember where we met him earlier on this road: a rich man, fasting, unable to eat his meal for remembering Mus'ab and his short cloak. He was afraid, he said, that his reward had come early. That is the second thing to notice. Wealth did not make him easy. It made him careful. Rich and giving, and still afraid his reward had come too soon.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, ONE OFFER.` · `WHERE IS YOUR MARKET?` · `CHEESE, BUTTER, AND A PROFIT.` · `RICH, AND STILL AFRAID.` · then, large: `RICH AND GIVING.`

segments.voice: The practice: give from a success. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that went well lately. A paycheck, a sale, a good grade, a job finished, a lucky break. Let yourself enjoy it for a breath. Then ask: what part of this could go to someone else? A bit of money to someone in need. Time, if money is tight. Credit, to the person who helped you get there. Breathe out, and choose one. If you pray, you can thank God for the success and ask that the giving be accepted. The bell holds the time.
Abd al-Rahman, servant of the Most Merciful, the emigrant who turned down half a fortune, asked for the market instead, and grew rich while staying generous. Today's word.
Your line: rich and giving. Today, take one thing that went right for you, and pass a piece of it on before the day ends. Day eight hundred forty, and a week of companions done.
